articles.title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
articles.summary: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.
articles.content:
Physicists at Northwestern University have achieved an unprecedented level of quantum control over a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists answer one of the most fundamental questions in physics: Why does the universe exist as we know it?

The researchers captured a rapidly moving positron produced through radioactive decay, slowed it down, and cooled it to a temperature just above absolute zero. They then confined the particle within a near-perfect vacuum, isolating it from ordinary matter, which would cause it to annihilate.

Using this approach, the team created what they call a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." Within this system, the positron behaves somewhat like an artificial atom, allowing researchers to observe and precisely manipulate its individual quantum energy levels.

The achievement lays the groundwork for what could become the most rigorous test yet of the fundamental symmetry between electrons and positrons. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that the two particles should behave as nearly perfect mirror images of each other.

By measuring the positron's magnetic properties with unprecedented accuracy and comparing them with those of an electron, scientists could uncover previously undetected differences. Any unexpected discrepancy would point to a weakness in the Standard Model and potentially offer clues to why the universe contains so much more matter than antimatter.

The research was published in Physical Review Letters.

"Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction," said Northwestern's Gerald Gabrielse, who led the study. "If you take an electron and an anti-electron (or positron) and collide them together, they both disappear. We describe that as annihilation, a concept that fuels science fiction writers' imaginations. The big mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we'd be left with nothing. There's clearly something wrong with that theory, and that's what we're trying to figure out."

Gabrielse is the Board of Trustees Professor of Physics at Northwestern's Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and director of the university's Center for Fundamental Physics. Thomas Myers, a Ph.D. student working in Gabrielse's laboratory, is the study's first author.

Searching for Cracks in the Standard Model

The Standard Model is one of the most successful theories in modern science. It describes the universe's fundamental particles and three of its four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces). Countless experiments have verified its predictions with remarkable accuracy.

Despite those successes, the theory remains incomplete. One of its most significant shortcomings is its inability to explain the overwhelming abundance of matter compared with antimatter in the observable universe.

"We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere -- or at least incomplete," Gabrielse said. "For example, it cannot predict why the universe exists, so that's a pretty big loophole. We're very precisely examining the most fundamental and simple systems to find where the theory breaks down. We hope to find an unambiguous answer."

Gabrielse has devoted decades of his scientific career to investigating this mystery. His research group previously developed methods for isolating individual electrons and determining their magnetic properties with exceptional precision.

He also helped establish the field of low-energy antimatter research by pioneering techniques for slowing, capturing, and cooling antiprotons. The latest achievement combines these two areas of expertise, extending the sophisticated quantum control previously demonstrated with electrons to an individual antimatter particle.

Trapping Antimatter Without Touching It

Almost everything on Earth is composed of three familiar particles: electrons, protons, and neutrons. A universe made of antimatter could contain their respective counterparts: positrons, antiprotons, and antineutrons. According to Gabrielse, if everything on Earth were constructed from antimatter instead of ordinary matter, distinguishing between the two would be remarkably difficult.

The dramatic differences emerge when matter and antimatter come into contact. An electron and a positron, for example, can annihilate when they encounter one another. This makes storing antimatter particularly challenging, as contact with the material walls of an ordinary container would almost certainly destroy the trapped particle.

"If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully," Gabrielse said. "To be clear, it's not dangerous. We don't have enough antimatter to make an explosion."

To overcome this problem, the Northwestern researchers employed an advanced particle trap that uses carefully configured electric and magnetic fields. These fields keep the positron suspended in an empty region of space, preventing it from coming into contact with the surrounding material.

By effectively creating a container that does not require the particle to touch any physical walls, the team has managed to keep a single positron confined in Gabrielse's laboratory for months.

Cooling Antimatter to Near Absolute Zero

Capturing a positron presents another considerable technical hurdle. Certain atomic nuclei release positrons as they undergo radioactive decay. For their experiment, the researchers used sodium-22, a rare radioactive isotope of sodium. Positrons emitted during this process initially carry tremendous amounts of energy.

The physicists substantially reduced the particle's speed before directing it into the trap's near-perfect vacuum. Inside, the temperature is maintained at approximately 300 millikelvins, equivalent to just 0.3 degrees above absolute zero.

Under these extremely cold conditions, the positron can settle into its lowest possible quantum energy state.

"We cool it down so much that it's in its quantum ground state," Gabrielse said. "We actually coaxed this very fast positron to sit there and behave for months at a time."

Putting Matter and Antimatter to the Ultimate Test

Beyond capturing and cooling the positron, the researchers demonstrated that they could deliberately change its individual quantum energy states and detect those changes.

Using microwaves tuned to specific frequencies, the physicists transferred carefully controlled amounts of energy to the particle and observed the resulting transitions between quantum states. This ability is crucial to their larger objective of determining the positron's magnetic properties with exceptional accuracy and comparing them directly with those of an electron.

In earlier research, Gabrielse and his colleagues used a one-electron quantum cyclotron to determine the electron's magnetic moment, a measure of its magnetic properties, with a precision of approximately one part in 10 trillion. That achievement ranks among the most precise measurements ever performed on an elementary particle.

The team now intends to conduct an equivalent measurement using the trapped positron. Comparing the two results could provide an extraordinarily sensitive test of current particle physics theories and potentially uncover evidence of previously unknown physics.

"Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements," Gabrielse said. "If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century."

The study, "One-positron quantum cyclotron," received support from the National Science Foundation (grant number 2110565).
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough in trapping and controlling antimatter (a positron) with unprecedented precision, enabling fundamental tests of particle physics that could explain why the universe exists. This advancement has broad implications for physics and our understanding of the universe, representing a major positive impact on science and society.
articles.personality_title: Scientists trap antimatter particle to unlock universe’s mysteries
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Physicists study antimatter, which is like ordinary matter but with opposite properties. When antimatter meets matter, they destroy each other. Understanding antimatter better could explain why the universe is made mostly of matter and not antimatter.

**What happened** – Researchers at Northwestern University successfully trapped a single positron, the antimatter partner of an electron. They slowed it down, cooled it to near absolute zero (very close to the coldest temperature possible), and kept it suspended in a special trap without touching any walls. This setup allowed them to control and observe the positron’s quantum energy levels for months.

**Impact** – This is the first time a positron has been held and controlled so precisely. By comparing the positron’s magnetic properties with those of an electron, scientists can test if the two particles behave exactly the same. If they find differences, it could reveal flaws in the Standard Model, the main theory describing particles and forces, and help explain why matter dominates the universe.

**What's next step** – The team will measure the positron’s magnetic properties with the highest precision ever and compare these to electron measurements. This could lead to new discoveries in physics and improve our understanding of the universe’s origins.

**One-sentence takeaway** – By trapping and studying a single antimatter particle with great precision, scientists are opening a new path to uncover why our universe exists as it does.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques piègent une particule d'antimatière pour percer les mystères de l'univers
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les physiciens étudient l'antimatière, qui est semblable à la matière ordinaire mais avec des propriétés opposées. Lorsque l'antimatière rencontre la matière, elles se détruisent mutuellement. Mieux comprendre l'antimatière pourrait expliquer pourquoi l'univers est principalement composé de matière.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs de l'université Northwestern ont réussi à piéger un positron, l'antiparticule de l'électron. Ils l'ont ralenti, refroidi près du zéro absolu (la température la plus basse possible) et maintenu suspendu dans un piège spécial sans contact avec les parois. Cela leur a permis de contrôler et d'observer les niveaux d'énergie quantique du positron pendant des mois.

**Impact** – C'est la première fois qu'un positron est retenu et contrôlé avec une telle précision. En comparant les propriétés magnétiques du positron à celles de l'électron, les scientifiques peuvent vérifier si les deux particules se comportent exactement de la même façon. Des différences pourraient révéler des failles dans le Modèle Standard, la théorie principale décrivant les particules et les forces, et aider à expliquer pourquoi la matière domine dans l'univers.

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos atrapan una partícula de antimateria para descubrir los misterios del universo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los físicos estudian la antimateria, que es como la materia normal pero con propiedades opuestas. Cuando la antimateria y la materia se encuentran, se aniquilan mutuamente. Entender mejor la antimateria podría explicar por qué el universo está formado principalmente por materia.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad Northwestern lograron atrapar un positrón, la antipartícula del electrón. Lo desaceleraron, enfriaron a casi el cero absoluto (la temperatura más baja posible) y lo mantuvieron suspendido en una trampa especial sin tocar paredes. Esto les permitió controlar y observar los niveles de energía cuántica del positrón durante meses.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que se sostiene y controla un positrón con tanta precisión. Al comparar las propiedades magnéticas del positrón con las del electrón, los científicos pueden comprobar si las dos partículas se comportan exactamente igual. Si encuentran diferencias, podrían revelar fallas en el Modelo Estándar, la teoría principal que describe partículas y fuerzas, y ayudar a explicar por qué la materia domina el universo.

**Próximo paso** – El equipo medirá las propiedades magnéticas del positrón con la mayor precisión jamás lograda y las comparará con las del electrón. Esto podría llevar a nuevos descubrimientos en física y mejorar nuestra comprensión del origen del universo.

**Resumen en una frase** – Al atrapar y estudiar una sola partícula de antimateria con gran precisión, los científicos abren un nuevo camino para descubrir por qué existe nuestro universo.

articles.title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
articles.summary: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.
articles.content:
Researchers at the University of Queensland have demonstrated an unusual new way to communicate, using gravity to send a message directly through a brick wall. Instead of relying on radio waves or other electromagnetic signals, the team used an old elevator, a massive counterweight, and an extremely sensitive instrument capable of detecting tiny changes in gravitational pull.

The experiment took place inside UQ's Parnell Building. Physicists repeatedly moved an elevator between two floors, shifting its 1.8-metric-ton counterweight between two positions. Each position represented a binary digit, either 0 or 1, allowing the researchers to encode information through the movement of the heavy mass.

On the other side of a brick wall, a device called a gravimeter was positioned in a nearby bathroom. The instrument measured the extremely small changes in gravity produced by the moving counterweight. By decoding those measurements, the team successfully recovered a one-word message: 'Gravity'.

Why Gravity Could Succeed Where Wi-Fi Fails

The experiment highlights a potentially important advantage of using gravity for communication. Unlike conventional wireless signals, which can be weakened or blocked by physical obstacles, gravitational fields pass through ordinary materials without being screened out.

Dr. Charles Woffinden from UQ's School of Mathematics and Physics explained why this property makes gravity an intriguing alternative to existing communication technologies.

"Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," Dr. Woffinden said.

"Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

"While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block."

The basic principle is surprisingly simple. Any object with mass produces a gravitational field, and moving that object changes the field around it. Although these changes are generally far too small for people to notice, sufficiently sensitive instruments can detect them. By controlling how a large mass moves, researchers can create a sequence of gravitational changes that represents digital information.

From Weighing Trucks to Sending Messages

The idea for the experiment emerged from a separate research effort that had little to do with communication.

Dr. Andrew Groszek said the team had originally been developing a contactless weighbridge, a system designed to measure the weight of vehicles without requiring them to drive onto a conventional scale.

"We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull," Dr. Groszek said.

"Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realized the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information."

That realization opened the door to a different application. If a sensitive detector could measure the gravitational influence of a large vehicle, it could also detect deliberately controlled changes in the position of a heavy object. Those changes could then be used to represent the ones and zeros that form the foundation of digital communication.

The Biggest Challenge Is Speed

Despite its success, the demonstration revealed a major obstacle to practical gravity-based communication: transmitting information this way is extraordinarily slow.

Professor Andrew White explained that the elevator's age and limited speed placed a severe restriction on how quickly the researchers could send their message.

"Our lift was snail-paced - it's from the 1950s - so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word," Professor White said.

For comparison, a bit is the smallest unit of digital information, representing either a 0 or a 1. Modern communication systems transmit enormous numbers of bits every second. The gravity experiment, by contrast, required an entire minute to communicate just one bit.

According to White, improving the system would require finding ways to produce detectable gravitational changes more quickly.

"The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it, and the sensitivity of the detector.

"It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future."

Could Quantum Sensors Make Gravity Communication Practical?

Although the experiment relied on a conventional gravity sensor, the researchers believe more advanced technology could eventually make the approach faster and capable of operating over greater distances.

Professor Matthew Davis emphasized that the team's most important achievement was demonstrating that gravity could be used to transmit recoverable information.

"It's not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating," Professor Davis said.

"We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

"Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters and data rates of around 15 bits per minute."

Quantum sensors exploit properties of quantum physics to make exceptionally precise measurements. In principle, their greater sensitivity could allow researchers to detect much smaller gravitational changes, potentially improving both the range and speed of gravity-based communication.

However, the team's projections depend on ambitious assumptions, and the suggested performance has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. Even at 15 bits per minute, the system would remain dramatically slower than modern wireless technologies.

Still, the potential applications are intriguing. A sufficiently advanced gravity-based communication system could someday transmit information in environments where radio waves, light, and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

For now, an aging elevator and a gravimeter in a university bathroom have demonstrated something remarkable: information can be carried by changes in gravity and recovered on the other side of a solid wall.

The research was published in Science Advances.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a novel scientific breakthrough demonstrating that gravity can be used to transmit information through solid barriers, overcoming limitations of conventional wireless communication. This has broad potential implications for future communication technologies, especially in challenging environments, and is supported by detailed experimental context and expert commentary.
articles.personality_title: Scientists send message through a brick wall using gravity
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists usually send messages with radio waves or Wi-Fi, but these signals can be blocked by walls or other objects. Gravity, the force that pulls objects together, passes through almost everything without being stopped.

**What happened** – At the University of Queensland, researchers used an old elevator’s heavy counterweight to send a message through a brick wall. They moved the 1.8-ton weight between two spots to create tiny changes in gravity. A special tool called a gravimeter on the other side of the wall detected these changes and decoded the message: the word "Gravity".

**Impact** – This experiment showed that gravity can carry information through solid objects that normally block wireless signals. This is important because it means we might one day communicate in places where Wi-Fi and radio don’t work, like inside tunnels or behind thick walls.

**What's next step** – Right now, sending messages with gravity is very slow—just one bit per minute—because the elevator moves slowly. Scientists hope to improve this by using bigger masses, faster movements, and more sensitive detectors, possibly with advanced quantum sensors. These improvements could allow gravity-based communication over longer distances and at faster speeds.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Researchers proved that moving heavy objects can send messages through walls using gravity, opening a new way to communicate where other signals fail.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques envoient un message à travers un mur en utilisant la gravité
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques utilisent généralement des ondes radio ou le Wi-Fi pour envoyer des messages, mais ces signaux peuvent être bloqués par des murs ou d’autres objets. La gravité, la force qui attire les objets, traverse presque tout sans être arrêtée.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – À l’Université du Queensland, des chercheurs ont utilisé le contrepoids lourd d’un vieil ascenseur pour envoyer un message à travers un mur en briques. Ils ont déplacé ce poids de 1,8 tonne entre deux positions pour créer de très petites variations de gravité. Un outil spécial appelé gravimètre, placé de l’autre côté du mur, a détecté ces changements et décodé le message : le mot « Gravité ».

**Impact** – Cette expérience a montré que la gravité peut transmettre des informations à travers des objets solides qui bloquent normalement les signaux sans fil. Cela signifie qu’un jour, on pourrait communiquer dans des endroits où le Wi-Fi et la radio ne fonctionnent pas, comme dans des tunnels ou derrière des murs épais.

**Prochaine étape** – Pour l’instant, envoyer des messages avec la gravité est très lent — un bit par minute — parce que l’ascenseur se déplace lentement. Les scientifiques espèrent améliorer cela en utilisant des masses plus grandes, des mouvements plus rapides, et des détecteurs plus sensibles, peut-être avec des capteurs quantiques avancés. Ces améliorations pourraient permettre une communication par gravité sur de plus longues distances et plus rapidement.

**En une phrase** – Les chercheurs ont prouvé que déplacer des objets lourds peut envoyer des messages à travers des murs grâce à la gravité, ouvrant une nouvelle manière de communiquer quand les autres signaux échouent.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos envían un mensaje a través de un muro usando gravedad
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Normalmente, los científicos envían mensajes con ondas de radio o Wi-Fi, pero estas señales pueden ser bloqueadas por paredes u otros objetos. La gravedad, la fuerza que atrae a los objetos, atraviesa casi todo sin detenerse.

**Qué pasó** – En la Universidad de Queensland, investigadores usaron el contrapeso pesado de un viejo ascensor para enviar un mensaje a través de un muro de ladrillos. Movieron ese peso de 1.8 toneladas entre dos posiciones para crear pequeños cambios en la gravedad. Un instrumento especial llamado gravímetro, ubicado al otro lado del muro, detectó estos cambios y descifró el mensaje: la palabra "Gravedad".

**Impacto** – Este experimento mostró que la gravedad puede transportar información a través de objetos sólidos que normalmente bloquean señales inalámbricas. Esto es importante porque significa que algún día podríamos comunicarnos en lugares donde el Wi-Fi y la radio no funcionan, como en túneles o detrás de paredes gruesas.

**Próximo paso** – Por ahora, enviar mensajes con gravedad es muy lento—solo un bit por minuto—porque el ascensor se mueve despacio. Los científicos esperan mejorar esto usando masas más grandes, movimientos más rápidos y detectores más sensibles, posiblemente con sensores cuánticos avanzados. Estas mejoras podrían permitir la comunicación por gravedad a mayores distancias y velocidades.

**Una frase clave** – Los investigadores demostraron que mover objetos pesados puede enviar mensajes a través de muros usando la gravedad, abriendo una nueva forma de comunicarse donde otras señales fallan.

articles.title: ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03835-0Awe, anxiety and opportunity: mathematics community shares mixed emotions following the solution of the field’s biggest unsolved problem.
articles.content:
Mathematics Álvaro Lozano-Robledo thought the Riemann hypothesis was out of AI’s reach for now.Credit: Bri Diaz/UConn Photo

The news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking. For months, reports have mounted of artificial-intelligence models toppling some of the toughest problems in mathematics, plunging the field into turmoil. But the latest claim was the most shocking yet: an AI model had helped to solve the field’s most famous open problem, the Riemann hypothesis.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The proof was released on 20 November by mathematician Levent Alpöge at AI giant Anthropic in San Francisco, California, who used an advanced version of the firm’s Claude model. It came in the form of 17 million lines of code in the open-source programming language Lean, which translates mathematical arguments into computer-certifiable code. In a matter of hours, a separate set of mathematicians rushed out a human-written proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which is in the branch of number theory and pertains to the randomness of prime numbers.

Alpöge’s proof has been independently verified by the non-profit organization behind Lean and the Mathlib Initiative, which runs the reference library of formalized mathematics results written in Lean. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him,” the community said in a statement on 21 November.

The mathematics community has broadly accepted the claim, although responses differ wildly. Some celebrate Alpöge’s achievement, but others see the development as proof that humans are fighting against machines for the future of mathematics.

Nature hears reactions from four mathematicians on what solving the Riemann hypothesis means to them.

Mathematician Tasmin Chu is part of the Association for Human Mathematics, whose members commit to doing AI-free research.Credit: Elizabeth Xiao

‘My reaction is grave concern’

Tasmin Chu, PhD student in mathematics at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena.

A technology that can autonomously prove the Riemann hypothesis is no trivial matter. I think that it is imperative our society acts to pause AI development as soon as possible. Over the past year, mathematical institutions have faced the impossible task of adapting to the rapidly changing capabilities of AI in real time.

It’s enormously disruptive for early-career researchers — the people who are the intellectual future of our field. Soon other sectors of society will face the same issues.

My reaction is grave concern. AI companies urgently require democratic oversight. I do not think AI’s encroachment into math is inevitable, nor is the death of human mathematical practice inevitable. It’s a choice to disempower ourselves, just as it’s a choice to continue building these technologies despite grave safety concerns. I continue to practice mathematics without LLMs, because I believe it’s critical that scientific inquiry continues in the hands of human beings. Many of us at the Association for Human Mathematics — whose organizing committee I am on — are collectively making the same decision.

‘It could present a great opportunity for discovery’

Harini Desiraju, postdoc in mathematics at the University of Warwick, UK.

Given the events of the past few months, this news wasn't entirely a surprise, but we need to wait to understand the Lean proof and let the experts verify it. It is several million lines of code, after all.

I am not a number theorist, so I might not have the same emotional attachment to the Riemann hypothesis. Nevertheless, I have deep appreciation for the ubiquity and the importance of the problem in several areas of maths and physics.

As for the recent events, I want to distinguish between formal proofs versus knowledge. It is an impressive feat to solve such a problem. However, because it is a Lean proof over millions of lines, it is going to take a while before the community gets real understanding, and validity of the proof. With an AI-independent approach available as well, it could present a great opportunity for discovery of new ideas and mathematics. We need to see how it all plays out.

There is another discussion to be had, which involves the role of frontier labs in research. Most of us see the potential benefits of this technology, but it is of utmost importance that we work towards a future where the agency is with the scientific community and not a couple of companies.

Mathematician Marcus Du Sautoy is anxious about what’s next for his field.Credit: David Levenson/Getty

‘Three months ago, I would have never predicted it’

Marcus Du Sautoy, mathematician and professor for the public understanding of science at the University of Oxford, UK.

It was real mix of emotions. A part of me says, how exciting to be alive when this great problem was solved! I think even when Fermat’s last theorem was solved, we had the same excitement and the same melancholy: that great motivator is gone.

Mixed in with that, is the complete surprise that it ended up being proved this way. If you’d asked me three months ago, I would never have predicted it.

There’s quite a lot of anxiety about what ‘math 2.0’ is going to look like.

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’

Xin Zhang, assistant professor in mathematics at the University of Hong Kong.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a groundbreaking achievement where AI has helped solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics' biggest unsolved problems. This represents a major breakthrough in AI-assisted scientific discovery with broad implications for mathematics and related fields. The proof has been independently verified, and the story contains detailed context about the event and its significance. Despite some concerns, the overall impact is inspiring and signals a transformative moment in technology and science.
articles.personality_title: AI helps solve the Riemann hypothesis, shaking up mathematics
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Riemann hypothesis is one of the biggest unsolved problems in mathematics. It deals with patterns in prime numbers, which are important in many areas like cryptography and computer science. For over 150 years, mathematicians have tried to prove it without success.

**What happened** – On November 20, 2026, mathematician Levent Alpöge used an advanced AI model called Claude, developed by the company Anthropic, to help prove the Riemann hypothesis. The AI created a proof written in a special computer language called Lean, which can check mathematical arguments automatically. Other mathematicians quickly wrote a version of the proof in regular math language. Independent groups confirmed the proof is correct.

**Impact** – This is the first time AI has solved such a famous and difficult math problem. It shows how AI can help humans make big scientific discoveries. Some mathematicians are excited because it might speed up research and lead to new ideas. Others worry that AI could change how math is done and affect the future of researchers, especially young ones.

**What's next step** – Mathematicians will study the AI-generated proof to fully understand it and explore new questions it raises. The math community must also decide how to use AI tools responsibly and balance human creativity with machine power. This moment might mark the start of a new era in mathematics and science.

**One-sentence takeaway** – An AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis marks a historic breakthrough, opening new paths for mathematical discovery and raising important questions about the future of research.

articles.title: The technology that could make government internet blackouts impossible
articles.summary: Direct-to-cell technology could one day provide a lifeline for getting around authoritarian regimes’ internet shutdowns, but international law and technical limitations are holding the technology back for now
articles.content:
Direct-to-cell technology could one day provide a lifeline for getting around authoritarian regimes’ internet shutdowns, but international law and technical limitations are holding the technology back for now

Protesters in London highlight the Iranian regime’s use of internet blackouts to crush dissent Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Shutterstock

An emerging satellite communication technology could curtail the ability of authoritarian regimes to cut off internet access to citizens.

Internet blackouts are a common fixture in countries like Myanmar, Pakistan, Ethiopia and Iran during periods of civil unrest, making organising any type of dissenting activity very difficult.

Iran’s regime, however, is worried that direct-to-cell (D2C) satellite internet will make it easier for citizens to escape restrictions. The country’s deputy communications minister, Mohammad Hafez Hakami, said on 30 September it may make blackouts impossible in the future by rendering current measures like device registration and user-identity verification ineffective, perhaps one day forcing the government to resort to more extreme measures like electricity blackouts.

Advertisement

Satellite internet, notably SpaceX’s Starlink, has already allowed some protesters and organisers in countries like Iran to weather internet blackouts by circumventing local carriers entirely.

However, the cost of a Starlink terminal needed to use the service can reportedly reach up to $4000 on the black-market Telegram chats where they are sold. Plus, the threat of potential jail time – up to two years in prison for possession in Iran – is a powerful deterrent.

D2C could change the game by letting standard, unmodified mobile phones connect to satellites in low Earth orbit, without any specialised hardware like a Starlink terminal or a satellite phone.

The satellites carry onboard mobile base stations, which act as cell towers in space, and currently broadcast on mobile operators’ ordinary ground spectrum. Companies like SpaceX and AST SpaceMobile are investing billions in getting the technology off the ground, with the promise of largely eliminating internet “dead zones” in rural areas where connectivity is unavailable or places where it has been cut off by natural disasters or power cuts.

Free newsletter Sign up to The Daily Sign up to newsletter

A basic version is already commercially available in the US through T-Mobile, mainly for texting and some low-bandwidth apps. SpaceX plans to start launching a next-generation constellation capable of broadband-style speeds during 2027, with commercial roll-out targeted for the first half of 2028.

Mahsa Alimardani, a researcher at the Oxford Internet Institute and founder of the D2C Coalition, sees the technology as a way to make services like Starlink more available to the wider population in countries like Iran. “You had to be privileged enough to afford Starlink, and it was really confined to the major cities like Tehran. It wasn’t an egalitarian tool,” she says. D2C technology could also be harder for the government to trace, as there is no large dish to hunt down.

But there are many technical issues that could stop D2C acting as a panacea for countries like Iran. The service as it is currently provided by Starlink and T-Mobile has a low bandwidth. Speeds average around 4 megabits per second per beam, which must be shared by users within the area, meaning limited capacity except for basic use cases like SMS messaging. The antenna on a mobile phone is much smaller than a Starlink terminal, limiting its ability to receive large amounts of data.

The other primary issue is overcoming the lack of permission and cooperation from a hostile host country. The satellite has to transmit in part of the radio spectrum that mobile phones can receive. If mobile operators in the country are already using that part of the spectrum, then the terrestrial signal would be much stronger than the satellite signal – so existing cell phone towers would effectively function as jammers.

“If there’s a tower down the road, it will overpower the satellite signal that’s going from hundreds of miles up in space,” says Tim Farrar at telecoms consultancy TMF Associates. “The link is already fragile.”

That could change in the future. Starlink’s next-generation D2C service will run on new frequency bands, the AWS-4 and H-block spectrum that SpaceX agreed to buy licences for in 2025. SpaceX is predicting speeds of 150 megabits per second under ideal conditions for its next-generation D2C Starlink service, roughly 38 times faster than current speeds. As the service will run on a different spectrum, existing cell towers in densely populated areas like Tehran will be unable to act as jammers.

SpaceX says it is working with chip-makers to get the necessary modems into next-generation smartphones. The firm’s CEO Elon Musk has predicted that it will take around two years for the mobile industry to start shipping compatible modems in their phones, but it could be a long time before those phones are available to ordinary Iranians.

The final issue is international law. Under the International Telecommunication Union’s radio regulations, transmitters operating on a country’s territory need that country’s authorisation. This has led the United Nations body to side with Iran in its complaints against Starlink. Digital rights groups, such as Witness, Access Now and Article 19, have been lobbying governments, regulators and satellite providers to allow US communications companies to switch on their D2C service over Iran since January 2026.

D2C technology could be a valuable tool for millions of people living under authoritarian regimes even with current technology, but the legal and technical hurdles mean its impact on internet blackouts will be limited for the foreseeable future.

“I suspect Iranian leadership’s concern is less about what direct-to-cell can actually do at the moment and more about where it’s going and what it might come to symbolise,” says Alimardani.

A satellite operator working without a licence and independently of the state, she argues, undermines Iran’s entire model of centralised internet governance, which helps explain the authorities’ efforts to seize the relatively small number of Starlink terminals already in the country.

“That is the fundamental thing that the regime has always sought to do: control communications. Control the narrative. Control the ability to mobilise and to organise. A channel that they can’t switch off is a direct challenge to that fundamental aspect of their system,” says Alimardani.

articles.personality_title: New satellite tech could stop governments from blocking internet access
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Some governments cut off internet access during protests or unrest to stop people from organizing or sharing information. This happens in countries like Iran, Myanmar, and Ethiopia, making it hard for citizens to communicate.

**What happened** – A new technology called direct-to-cell (D2C) satellite internet could allow regular mobile phones to connect directly to satellites in space without special equipment. Companies like SpaceX and AST SpaceMobile are working on this technology. Currently, it is available in a simple form in the US with limited speed, but better versions are planned by 2027.

**Impact** – D2C could make it much harder for governments to block internet access because it does not rely on local cell towers. People could use their normal phones to get online even if the government shuts down regular internet. This could help many people in places where internet blackouts are common, allowing better communication during emergencies or protests.

**What's next step** – The technology still faces challenges like low current speeds, legal restrictions from governments, and technical issues with local signals overpowering satellite signals. SpaceX plans to launch faster D2C services using new radio frequencies, and phone makers will need to build compatible devices. Activists are pushing for international permission to use D2C in restricted countries.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Direct-to-cell satellite internet could soon let people bypass government internet shutdowns using regular phones, but legal and technical hurdles remain before it becomes widely available.

articles.personality_title_es: Nueva tecnología satelital podría impedir que gobiernos bloqueen el acceso a internet
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Algunos gobiernos cortan el acceso a internet durante protestas o disturbios para evitar que las personas se organicen o compartan información. Esto ocurre en países como Irán, Myanmar y Etiopía, dificultando la comunicación.

**Qué pasó** – Una nueva tecnología llamada internet satelital directa a celular (D2C) podría permitir que teléfonos móviles normales se conecten directamente a satélites en el espacio sin equipos especiales. Empresas como SpaceX y AST SpaceMobile están desarrollando esta tecnología. Actualmente está disponible en Estados Unidos en una versión básica con velocidad limitada, pero se planean mejores versiones para 2027.

**Impacto** – D2C podría dificultar mucho que los gobiernos bloqueen el acceso a internet porque no depende de las torres locales. Las personas podrían usar sus teléfonos normales para conectarse, incluso si el gobierno apaga el internet tradicional. Esto podría ayudar a muchas personas en lugares donde los apagones de internet son comunes, permitiendo mejor comunicación en emergencias o protestas.

**Próximo paso** – La tecnología aún enfrenta desafíos como velocidades bajas, restricciones legales y problemas técnicos con señales locales que pueden bloquear las señales satelitales. SpaceX planea lanzar servicios D2C más rápidos usando nuevas frecuencias, y los fabricantes de teléfonos deberán crear dispositivos compatibles. Activistas están presionando para obtener permiso internacional para usar D2C en países restringidos.

**Resumen en una frase** – El internet satelital directo a celular podría permitir pronto a las personas evitar apagones de internet con teléfonos normales, pero aún quedan obstáculos legales y técnicos por superar.
